📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United are like John Toshack’s duvet. You fix one problem – being far too vulnerable to conceding goals – only to create another – lacking the threat to score. It is all very Meh United not Man United. The indisputable fact is they are just not very entertaining to watch. They are slow and dull.

Industry observers note that in the end it also points to another thing. The thing highlighted in midweek by Lisandro Martínez after the Champions League defeat at Atlético Madrid: they do not have the strength in depth to compete.

According to recent reports, what they do have appears to not be fit for purpose. Certainly Michael Carrick, the under-pressure manager, is struggling to get the best out of the resources he has.

Sources indicate that “It’s like a duvet,” Toshack, the former Real Madrid and Wales manager, famously mentioned of football. “If you pull it up, your feet get cold. If you pull it down, your shoulders get cold.”.

There will have been times in the last few days, with the intense criticism and scrutiny over his future, when Carrick will have simply felt like dragging that duvet up over his head and keeping it there.

Defeat by Leeds United would have been unthinkable. It would have put Carrick under potentially intolerable pressure in what appears to be a pivotal week, with Como away in the Champions League and a home Premier League fixture against Bournemouth in the coming days.

It has been revealed that was this a lifeline or the tightening of the noose for Carrick? Time will soon tell. The relief of avoiding defeat was tempered by the reality of it now being just one win in their opening seven league games – at home to newly promoted Ipswich Town – and they are down in 13th place. It is six games without a win in all competitions.

That is unacceptable and is their fewest number of league victories in a top-flight campaign since 1986-87. Back then they sacked their manager in November and brought in a certain Alex Ferguson.

The hard truth is Carrick needs to start collecting some “Ws” in those results columns. United are already 14 points behind leaders Manchester City and five outside the probable Champions League places. Qualifying again for that tournament must be the minimum expectation.

Ruben Amorim, Carrick’s predecessor, lost his job within 24 hours of the same 1-1 scoreline at Elland Road last season – dismissed after Martínez-like explosive comments again aimed at director of football Jason Wilcox. Carrick will not suffer the same fate after this, but the ice is becoming increasingly thin.

According to recent reports, we have seen this movie before at United. A slow start to the season, a period of drift, falling out of contention, no reaction on the pitch, backing from the hierarchy that becomes increasingly unconvincing. And then a change.

According to recent reports, can Carrick, who genuinely does still retain support at the highest level, alter that pattern? Does he have it in him? Is he too passive like his team? Carrick said this draw felt like a “fresh start”, but on this evidence that comment can be classified as wildly optimistic.

Having directed his criticism at the United hierarchy, and specifically Wilcox, the former Leeds winger who was here, over a lack of summer signings, Martínez apologised and was named in the starting XI. But the Argentine only lasted to half-time, withdrawn injured with a tight thigh, and sat watching the second half with his hood up over his head.

What United did sign in the last window was three midfielders – at a cost of £155m – and all three started: Carlos Baleba alongside Andrey Santos with Youri Tielemans in the No 10 role, which meant Bruno Fernandes was pushed out to the left, from where he constantly wanted to come in-field, with Amad Diallo on the right.

Carrick talked of having a “fresh spine” as well as that fresh start. But it did not make for a potent combination even if, further forward, Bryan Mbeumo played through the middle and scored one. He should have scored another.

In a recent development, bryan Mbeumo finds the net this time to put Manchester United 1-0 up at Leeds! 🔴 https://t.co/NKDIhlUND1.

According to recent reports, but beyond that United created little. “It was a dominant performance against Man United,” Daniel Farke, the Leeds manager, claimed. He was right. If one team deserved to win it was his. They had the chances but snatched at them with Anton Stach, in injury time, having a weak shot cleared off the line by Martínez’s replacement Noussair Mazraoui after a mistake by goalkeeper Senne Lammens. Stach had to score.

United were ahead at half-time. Mbeumo had headed wastefully wide when unmarked but did well to force his way past James Justin and meet a low cross from Tielemans to poke the ball home. The way the usually undemonstrative Carrick punched the air in his technical area revealed the pressure he felt. It was something to build on. To gain control.

Recent findings suggest that leeds had started well but did not really pose much of a threat – beyond forcing Lammens to save well from Nico Elvedi’s downward header – and maybe the earlier kick-off subdued the crowd. This was far from a bear pit.

But after the break, Leeds were comfortably the better side. The nature of their equalising goal, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin too strong and alert for first Baleba and then Mbeumo to fire in from a corner, exposed the enduring softness at the heart of United.

Dominic Calvert-Lewin equalises for Leeds against Manchester United 👊 https://t.co/mnpyxZJKbm.

And that must be addressed by Carrick, especially as he appeared to sacrifice attacking intent by shoring up defensively. But that duvet is looking far too inadequate right now. Or Carrick is making it appear so.

Michael Carrick says he has put on “the headphones” this week in an effort to drown out the noise, but admitted Manchester United have to stop their struggles from snowballing.

United sit just two points above the relegation zone after a 1-1 draw at Leeds left them with just one win from their opening seven Premier League matches.

Carrick claimed the result felt like a “fresh start” after a week in which Lisandro Martínez publicly apologised for criticising Jason Wilcox, the United director of football, and the Old Trafford board.

But the United manager acknowledged their position “doesn’t look too good” and that they must start winning soon to stop the club from entering another doom cycle.

“Listen, we’re not accepting it as everything’s great by any stretch, so I’m realistic with that,” said the United manager, who claimed “the headphones have been on this week”.

Industry observers note that “But sometimes you do struggle, sometimes there’s a bit of it where you have to find a way through it. We haven’t really had to go through that yet [before now] and we have to find a way through it.

Sources indicate that “There has been a cycle at times here over a period of time when it can go in different directions. We’ve got to be stable enough to keep doing the right things for the right reasons as a group, and we’re more than capable of winning football matches.

“I understand the situation doesn’t look too good if you look at it from a certain way, but I’ve no doubts we can go on a good run.”.

United face Como in the Champions League in Italy on Wednesday before Bournemouth visit Old Trafford four days later.

It has been revealed that carrick said he remains convinced United can still have a strong campaign, despite their worst start to a season for 40 years. I know what we’ve got in the changing room, where we want to get to, how we want to get there,” he said. “We know we can do it.

“We’ve done it for some time, and we feel we’re a better group now, and I do feel that. Sometimes it doesn’t always show, but you get a feeling and I’m encouraged by a lot of things. And if we keep doing the right things, I think we can still have a really good season.”.

Asked if he would be putting the headphones back on this week ahead of two more pivotal games, Carrick added: “Nah, it’s always quiet for me.”.

Industry observers note that martínez was substituted at half-time at Elland Road with a tight thigh just days after his tirade at club executives and Marcus Rashford was left out for “purely tactical” reasons. “Nothing personal, the front players were doing a good job on and off the ball,” Carrick said. “Everyone is ready for Wednesday.”.

According to recent reports, the Leeds boss told Sky Sports: “We are slightly disappointed it is just a point. Overall, I felt it was not necessary to be losing at half time but it is still Manchester United. Second half, we got the equaliser, we should have kept up the dominance, too many strikes went over the crossbar but it was overall a solid performance. We should have won the game but we move on.

According to recent reports, “We took it as a compliment that we have done many things right over the last month if we were seen as favourites against Manchester Untiedbut we have earned this. We wanted to prove the comments right.

“We were the dominant side but we couldn’t capitalise as we lacked quality in and around the box.

Recent findings suggest that “It notes a lot about how much respect we have earned. Overall, this is where we are at the moment and overall, it is a good place to be.

According to recent reports, “It is still difficult in this league to win points. You have to be clinical and be very, very effective but we have to keep going.”.

Sources indicate that speaking to Sky Sports, he stated: “I think we could’ve played with a bit more quality in the final third, particularly in the first half. We were getting good quality in the box but just not enough numbers.

Industry observers note that “We made sure in the second half we came out with more confidence going forward. I think we were unlucky not to win the game.

“They tried to [match us up formation-wise]. Not surprised given what happened last season. They were probably looking at our physical output and the way we liked to play and tried to go man-for-man.

Recent findings suggest that “It took us a little bit to adjust to it, but I don’t think it was too difficult to adjust. It was more down to us and maybe a lack of quality in the final third.”.

Tottenham star Tosin Adarabioyo has joined forces with former Chelsea team-mates Reece James and Levi Colwill to launch a trading card shop in London.

Card Cop, opening in Borough Market on Thursday, will sell cards from a variety of sports as well as other collections such as Pokemon and Marvel.

Industry observers note that adarabioyo began collecting as a child and returned to the hobby in 2020. His collection, which he shares on social media, spans a variety of sports and he also has several of Brazilian icon Neymar.

'I’ve been collecting for years, and it’s great to see the hobby continue to grow,' remarked the 29-year-old, who left Chelsea for Spurs last summer.

'I love collecting. It’s a great way for supporters to connect with their favourite players. I’ve always felt that collectors are some of the most passionate fans.

Recent findings suggest that 'I’ve got to know so many collectors through the hobby. Talking about our collections is an instant icebreaker, and I know those conversations can mean a lot. I want to bring more players into the hobby and recreate those moments.

Tosin Adarabioyo, like many footballers, has a passion for collecting trading cards.

The new shop is set to open in London's Borough Market next week.

Adarabioyo enjoyes collecting cards of former PSG star Neymar, who won 130 caps for Brazil.

'Neymar is criminally underrated to me, and I think his cards are too. Some of the images take me straight back to performances I’ve watched over the years. It’s hard to describe, but it’s like bottling up that feeling forever. Football purists will know what I mean.'.

West Ham defender Kyle Walker-Peters, who played with Tosin at England youth level, is among backers along with James and Colwill.

Adarabioyo already has an online retail business, The Huddle, with guests such as Dominic Solanke, Robert Sanchez and Adam Wharton all featuring on live streams, opening boxes as fans watch.

Recent figures valued the global sports trading card market at $13.75billion (£10.5bn) in 2025, with that projected to grow to $27.52bn (£21bn) by 2034.

Formula One star Lewis Hamilton got in on the act earlier this year, launching his own venture and a shop in Frankfurt.

The seven-time world champion was already an ambassador for Topps - who also have the licence for Premier League cards - and remarked: 'I’ve loved collecting cards since I was a kid — Pokemon, football, anything I could get my hands on.

According to recent reports, 'To now play a role in shaping the future of the category is incredible. We have a significant opportunity to tap into the culture in a way no one has before.'.

Three of Everton's Premier League fixtures in January – including the Merseyside derby at Anfield – have been moved for live television coverage.

The Toffees' trip to Coventry City remains on Saturday 16 January, but with an earlier kick-off time of 12.30pm (GMT), and will be shown live on TNT Sports.

The following weekend, David Moyes' side will now host Brentford at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Sunday 24 January, in a 2pm (GMT) kick-off that will be broadcast live on Sky Sports.

Finally, the Merseyside derby against Liverpool at Anfield on Saturday 30 January will now take place at the earlier time of 12.30pm (GMT) and will be live on TNT Sports.

Keep an eye on evertonfc.com and the Club's social media channels for ticketing updates.

Breaking: AI must be held accountable — value statements won’t protect human dignity

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (757 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • There is a striking gap in debates about artificial intelligence.
  • Industry observers note that in September, the UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights published its report on AI regulation.
  • AI governance requires more than just a declaration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There is a striking gap in debates about artificial intelligence. Policy bodies and frontier AI laboratories are borrowing the vocabulary of legal constitutions to guide model development and oversight. However, these statements currently don’t include the institutional safeguards that would make such value commitments work.

Industry observers note that in September, the UK Parliament’s Joint Committee on Human Rights published its report on AI regulation. It uses ‘human rights’ more than 100 times in as many pages, but doesn’t discuss which rights should be protected or how. AI firm Anthropic in San Francisco, California, has written a ‘constitution’ for its model Claude. In it, numerous values are listed as the tool’s priorities, including the preservation of user autonomy. Yet some of these values, such as autonomy and well-being, compete with each other, as Anthropic acknowledges. The document does not provide an independent arbiter to adjudicate the conflict, or monitor violations by the AI system.

AI governance requires more than just a declaration. It requires a system of accountability. Specific institutions should constrain the tools’ influence in accordance with specific fundamental values and hold firms accountable to individuals affected by AI transgressions. Lawyers call this constitutionalism.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

AI is set to completely transform cybersecurity — here’s how researchers must prepare.

As a scholar of constitutional law, I see parallels between the current debate on AI governance and how national constitutions have been crafted, broken, borrowed and fixed.

Countries’ constitutions have distinct underlying priorities affecting their design. These fall roughly into two historical approaches (C. Skach Int. J. Const. Law 7, 175–181; 2009). One takes liberty as its priority: describing what people are free to do and what the state should not do to interfere. The other focuses on human dignity: noting not what individuals may do, but what cannot be done to them, regardless of the circumstances or whether they have consented to it.

Industry observers note that germany’s post-war constitutionalism demonstrates the latter. Its founding document, or basic law, was designed in 1949 to put dignity first and foremost — as both the highest guiding value and a constitutional right, the violation of which is actionable in court. It established an independent federal constitutional court, which citizens can approach directly, that became operational two years later. The choice of this value and the legal institutions to protect it were a response to the atrocities of the Nazi regime, in which people became instruments of state objectives.

Frontier AI companies and policymakers should seriously consider using these features of German constitutionalism. When dignity as a constitutional right is violated — by an AI-generated deepfake or by a chatbot that treats a distressed user as just another interaction — the people affected could petition the court directly, and the perpetrator could be stopped and held accountable.

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents.

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents.

Breaking: EU moves to loosen rules on pesticide use as experts sound the alarm

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1176 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation.
  • Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.
  • In a recent development, the European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as part of its drive to "streamline and simplify" EU laws, the European Commission has proposed sweeping changes for agriculture and food safety legislation. These include a move to ease rules controlling the use of pesticides and herbicides, which help fight pests and weeds.

Under current EU rules, which date back to 2011, primary pesticide components, or active substances, are only granted approval for limited periods of no more than 15 years.

In a recent development, the European Commission's proposed revamp of the system would make indefinite greenlighting — including of the controversial glyphosate, which has been linked to cancer and kills almost all plant life — the default. Safety reviews would only be done in exceptional cases, and regulatory authorities, not the industry, would bear responsibility.

In a recent development, the commission has remarked its goal is to cut costs, simplify work for authorities and help farmers stay competitive. Scientists and doctors, however, warn that concerns over human health and environmental impact from these toxic substances are being brushed aside.

The European Commission has said it's responding to complaints from farmers and the agriculture industry to clarify EU rules that govern pesticide use.

A joint statement released in May by 19 food associations, including CropLife Europe, which promotes pesticides, said complicated administrative procedures and a lengthy approvals process meant farmers were "left without any effective solutions to protect their crops against insects, weeds and diseases," putting food security and livelihoods at risk.

"The existing system of periodic renewal assessment of every active substance has become unsustainable," the commission's press service told DW, citing "chronic delays" and "bottlenecks" in the approval of fresh, more sustainable products.

In recent negotiations, EU member states noted open-ended authorizations should be restricted to "low-risk active substances.".

But their stance is still wanting to extend initial approval periods for other substances to up to 15 years, and a maximum of 25 years for renewals.

Herbert Dorfmann, a center-right Italian member of the European Parliament, said there is presently a yearslong delay in approving newly introduced pesticides, including more eco-friendly options, meaning farmers are forced to rely on older substances. Or, if these are banned, go without altogether.

The commission wants to "make the system more efficient and responsive," while guaranteeing that "the protection of human and animal health and the environment remain the highest priorities.".

Dorfmann, who as co-rapporteur is responsible for interinstitutional negotiations on the matter, backs the commission's stance, saying the EU needs "to open up the system for innovation.".

He aims to bring the parliament's proposal on the newly introduced pesticide rules to a vote among EU lawmakers before the end of the year.

Ecologists and medical experts, however, have spoken out forcefully against the proposed changes, saying the potential implications for human health and the environment are being downplayed.

In September, more than 500 experts from across the EU signed an open letter calling on the European Parliament to suspend its consideration of the latest regulations and conduct an independent investigation into health and environmental impacts.

On October 7, UN rights experts also backed the call for a full review into whether the proposed changes violated the EU's obligations under international human rights law, especially with regard to agricultural workers and children.

Pesticides can persist in the environment, contaminating water and degrading soils. They can also drive biodiversity loss and poison other animals higher up the food chain.

When it comes to humans, the European Environment Agency has said it was "not yet possible to estimate the burden of disease linked to current levels of exposure to all pesticides.".

However, exposure to chemical pesticides, including banned substances that still persist in the environment, has been linked to various cancers, chronic respiratory disease, neurological disorders and developmental delays, as well as problems with fertility and behavior.

And exposure is widespread: A survey conducted between 2014 and 2021 found that 84% of urine samples from both children and adults in five European countries contained residue from two or more pesticides.

Martina Vijver, scientific director and ecotoxicology expert at Leiden University in the Netherlands, remarked experts were "deeply concerned" that the EU's current plan "will weaken rather than strengthen the level of protection for pesticide regulation.".

Speaking at the European Parliament in September, she noted regular reassessments were key to evaluating the safety of pesticides with new findings, pointing out that the perception of risk changes over time.

"The regulatory system must remain capable of correcting yesterday's decisions with tomorrow's knowledge," she mentioned.

Salome Roynel, a policy officer at the Pesticide Action Network Europe, an NGO based in Brussels, said the harmful effects of pesticides aren't often fully understood until years later, when the product is up for reconsideration.

"Upcoming science emerges all the time," she told DW, highlighting how 56 active substances have been banned in the EU since 2011 as a result of periodic reviews.

That includes the insecticide chlorpyrifos, previously used in orchards and on vegetable and cereal crops, which has been tied to harmful effects on children's brain development.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Roynel mentioned it was "obvious that there was some kind of alignment" between the changes proposed by the EU institutions and the demands of the pesticide lobby.

This echoes a latest report by nonprofit research and campaign group Corporate Europe Observatory, which said Dorfmann and other lawmakers had "copy-pasted […] industry demands" into their regulatory proposals.

Dorfmann denied the lobby influence, telling DW he had met with "both sides, industry and environmental associations," in public debates on the matter.

In a recent development, "The main objective is not to keep old products in the market. The main objective is to bring latest ones to the market," Dorfmann mentioned.

Part of that blueprint, he added, would be to help more environmentally friendly "biocontrol" products and low-risk substances to bypass current administrative hurdles and get on the market faster.

It's an idea previously championed by Vijver, who agrees that the current system means more environmentally friendly pesticides are stuck in an administrative "traffic jam." She told DW that biocontrol products could go in a green "bus lane" to ease the way to approval at the European Food Safety Authority, while maintaining crucial safety reviews to filter out the more dangerous products.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Roynel also supports the initiative to speed up approval for biocontrol substances, but mentioned it needs to be part of a wider system change that includes financial support, monitoring and training to use these newly introduced products, as well as maintaining the restrictions on more harmful chemical pesticides ― not further deregulation.

"If farmers get easier access to synthetic pesticides tomorrow, they would have no incentive to switch to biocontrol," she said. "It's vital to put [biocontrol pesticides] on the market and we fully support that, but… it will not be the silver bullet.".

Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany.
  • According to recent reports, they only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow.
  • In a recent development, the scientists see the work as critical.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

According to recent reports, they only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

In a recent development, the scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, notes she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.

"That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped.".

It has been revealed that underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.

Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," mentioned Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance.".

Recent findings suggest that but the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.

Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.

In a recent development, "Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he stated.

The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.

Recent findings suggest that "We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig stated.

Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing fresh ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.

Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.

According to recent reports, "Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.

"The major advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity.".

Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.

Recent findings suggest that they then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the fresh crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.

According to recent reports, "We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen mentioned. "It's looking really good.".

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reworded scientific phrases can thwart publishers’ plagiarism checkers, but, in many cases, the resulting combinations of words only draw more attention from scientific sleuths.
  • According to recent reports, these days, I spend a lot of my time looking through published papers that I suspect are fraudulent.
  • I retired in 2022 from the University of Oxford, UK, where I worked as a developmental neuropsychologist.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reworded scientific phrases can thwart publishers’ plagiarism checkers, but, in many cases, the resulting combinations of words only draw more attention from scientific sleuths. Credit: Gregory Dubus/iStock via Getty.

According to recent reports, these days, I spend a lot of my time looking through published papers that I suspect are fraudulent. It is a gruelling task. But amid the tedium, there is some light relief, thanks to some hilarious phrases used by authors seeking to avoid detection by plagiarism checkers. It’s hard not to smile when ‘breast cancer’ becomes ‘bosom peril’, or a citation for ‘Baker and Logue’ become ‘Pastry Specialist and Logue’.

I retired in 2022 from the University of Oxford, UK, where I worked as a developmental neuropsychologist. I now track down research fraud as part of a community of scientific sleuths. We work together to identify papers that we consider to be problematic in some way, then send the evidence to publishers or post it on PubPeer, a post-publication peer-review platform. Our aim is for the problematic papers to be investigated and, if appropriate, retracted by their publishers. But, often, publishers are slower and more recalcitrant than many sleuths would like them to be.

‘A waste of time for all of us’: caught in the crossfire of the peer-review wars.

‘A waste of time for all of us’: caught in the crossfire of the peer-review wars.

Many people blame academia’s ‘publish or perish’ research culture for the rise in problematic papers. Without a large number of publications and citations, prospects for employment, promotion and glittering prizes evaporate. Some researchers cut corners, manipulate or fabricate data, or copy the work of other scientists without citing them.

The demand for desperate researchers to get their name on a publication in any journal has spawned semi-professional organizations known as paper mills. These sell authorship status, with prices that vary depending on the impact factor of the journal. Articles are typically generated using artificial-intelligence tools or plagiarized, and tend to find homes in journals that lack sufficient editorial scrutiny.

Sources indicate that one of the few amusing consequences of these developments is the phenomenon of tortured phrases, first described in 2021 by computer scientists Guillaume Cabanac and Cyril Labbé and software engineer Alexander Magazinov1. They analysed huge volumes of research literature to identify patterns. Tortured phrases arise when someone — or, in most cases, a computer — replaces words in a published article with synonyms to evade plagiarism detectors and ultimately publish the result as their own work.

Authorship for sale: Nature investigates how paper mills work.

Authorship for sale: Nature investigates how paper mills work.

In a recent development, cabanac and colleagues developed a free website called the Problematic Paper Screener, which documents tortured phrases and other red flags in publications. Detection of tortured phrases has been a communal effort by research sleuths, who document specific articles with tortured phrases on PubPeer.

This season’s Premier League title race may be locked in a paralysed state of uncertainty but Arsenal, the defending champions, are determined to keep it interesting.

While the painful delay on Manchester City’s battle against their guilty verdict threatens to drag deep into next year, Arsenal are remaining hot on their tails.

City’s lead at the top is back to three points but Arsenal’s win here was unlikely to have sent any shivers down the spines of Enzo Maresca and his players in this phoney mess of a season.

It was not until the 80th minute that Arsenal finally registered their first shot on target, and that was the moment which ended their cycle of frustration at the City Ground.

Just when it appeared Mikel Arteta was heading for a third successive goalless draw at the home of Nottingham Forest, substitute Noni Madueke’s deflected strike proved the difference.

Regardless, Mikel Arteta and his Arsenal players have their own motivations to accumulate as many points as possible before January as they seek to retain the title for the first time since the 1930s.

Recent findings suggest that arsenal have struggled at the City Ground, drawing 0-0 on their last two Premier League visits. They also lost at Forest in May 2023, a result which confirmed Manchester City as champions at Arsenal’s expense, and were knocked out of the FA Cup by Forest in January 2022.

Forest are yet to score a home league goal under Oliver Glasner, another data point suggesting this will be a low-scoring game.

That might not be the full story though, with Forest creating a hatful of chances in their defeat at Crystal Palace last week and Arsenal also playing a more inventive, technical game with the ball so far this season.

Arsenal have yet to score from a non-penalty set-piece, and their percentage of goals from open play is now the highest in the Premier League.

Morgan Gibbs-White is a doubt after sustaining what Glasner described as a “minor muscle injury” at Palace and his involvement in the game will be a last-minute call. With the exception of Christos Tzolis, Piero Hincapie and long-term absentee William Saliba, Arsenal’s squad is in pretty good health. Bukayo Saka, Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz, Riccardo Calafiori and Ben White could be recalled to Arteta’s starting XI after starting the Champions League win over Lille on the bench.

Full team news on the way shortly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Volkswagen Group on Thursday posted its worst quarterly numbers in more than a decade.

The tech giant reported an operating loss of €5.86 billion (roughly $6.53 billion) during July, August and September. One-off costs, not least a massive writedown in its stake in struggling sister company Porsche, explained the vast bulk of the losses.

The world's second-largest carmaker is battling mounting competition from and falling demand in the core Chinese market.

It is pursuing a major restructuring and downsizing program, trying to bolster falling profit margins, and executives said the difficulties highlighted the urgency of this process.

Industry observers note that "The nine-month results make one thing clear: We cannot afford to lose any time. We must act quickly and decisively," chief financial officer Arno Antlitz said in a video statement.

The results were the latest reminder of the pressure on VW — and the wider German and Western automotive industry — to react to increasing competition in China, high costs and practical difficulties moving towards electric car production, and unpredictable and rising tariff burdens, thanks in no small part to US President Donald Trump.

Here are some of the key Q3 figures:.

And here are some of the key year-to-date 9-month figures:.

VW shares were already at their lowest levels in well over 10 years prior to Thursday's announcements, after months of difficult headlines and the ongoing intends to shed tens of thousands of jobs and reduce production capacities.

Perhaps as a result of this, the stock dipped briefly as markets opened and the news was published, but then started to rally as the day progressed.

By midday in Frankfurt, VW shares had climbed by 2% compared to their prices at the start of trading on the DAX.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

CEO Oliver Blume aims to shed around 100,000 jobs across the group, which includes the Audi and Porsche brands, in the coming years though a combination of layoffs and not replacing departing or retiring personnel.

It has been revealed that multiple factors are contributing to this. They include increased competition from Chinese manufacturers, falling revenues in China, changeable US auto tariffs under President Donald Trump, different staffing requirements when manufacturing electric cars and difficulties moving towards making and selling more electric cars at the pace once designated by political leaders.

Up to four plants in Germany could face closure as part of the proposal, which has met with considerable union resistance and could lead to strikes starting next year.

CFO Antlitz said the figures demonstrated the urgency underlying these plans, saying the company needed to increase its profit margins by 2030 to solidify its finances.

Antlitz stated the operating return on sales was only 3.8% in the first nine months of the year, even before the one-off writedowns hitting the bottom line.

"That is not enough in the long term," he said.

As part of its restructuring program, the VW Group aims to restore an operating profit margin of between 8-10% by 2030.

This year, amid one-off costs now totaling in the region of €10 billion, it expects a profit margin of no more than 1%, compared to prior forecasts in the region of 5%.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.
  • India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

India's Ministry of Finance expects India's economy to grow at a pace of 7.3% in the current fiscal year based on its latest assessment of current data, it mentioned in its October economic review.

The estimate is a slight increase on the previous forecast of 7.1%.

India's current fiscal year, known as FY27, runs from April 1, 2026 to March 31, 2027.

The report contrasted these figures with global growth predictions of nearer 3%, saying "India's growth momentum, by comparison, has held firm.".

The ministry said growth in various key indicators like energy consumption, port traffic, goods and services tax (GST) collections, and car sales had accelerated in the previous quarter.

However, the ministry also warned of continued inflationary pressure and pressure on the rupee currency, as well as downside risks from the El Nino weather phonemenon that could threaten soil moisture ahead of the winter sowing season.

It said that external factors like oil prices and "global uncertainties" — seemingly a reference at least in part to the instablity in the Middle East — continued to pressure the rupee's value and pose inflationary risks.

Consumer price inflation (CPI), the wholesale price index (WPI), food cost prices and fuel and power prices were all rising month for month, albeit at very different rates.

It has been revealed that the CPI was up 5.54% year-on-year in September, but the WPI had risen more sharply at 11.39%. Food index inflation was up by 8% in rural areas, and a slightly more modest 7.18% in urban centers.

But, as in many other countries, fuel and power costs increases were in an entirely different league, at 25.85% inflation in September 2026 comapred to the same month a year earlier, prior to the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East.

Although it has been a comparatively slow decline, the rupee has been consistently losing value against the US dollar over the past five years, threatening the country's relative purchasing power internationally. This slide has picked up pace in the last 15 months or so.

But the ministry pointed to foreign exchange reserves worth some $721 billion and noted that India was "well-positioned" to weather such risks and sustain its expansionary trajectory..

  • For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.
  • In a recent development, in Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For Star Trek fans, he was the legendary Captain Picard; the British actor and director Patrick Stewart, longtime member of the  Royal Shakespeare Company, died on Thursday at the age of 86 following a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy body dementia, according to an official statement on his social media accounts.

In a recent development, in Los Angeles, California, far away from the small English village of Mirfield where he was born, Stewart achieved world fame. He was 47 years old when he landed the role of a lifetime in the legendary science fiction series Star Trek: Playing Captain Jean-Luc Picard in "Star Trek: The Next Generation," he stepped into the shoes of the legendary Captain James T. Kirk, played by William Shatner.

Stewart brought a calm, measured and distinctly British presence that quickly made Picard a fan favorite and a cult figure in the Star Trek universe. He returned to the role decades later in the spin-off series "Star Trek: Picard," which ended in 2023, proving the character's enduring appeal.

As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, he led the crew of the starship Enterprise, a spaceship with the sizeable mission: "To explore strange upcoming worlds. To seek out new life and new civilizations" — and most importantly, "to boldly go where no man has gone before!".

Recent findings suggest that stewart's interest in acting was sparked in the early 1950s when a teacher asked him to recite a work by Shakespeare. His passion for Shakespeare stayed with him until the end.

His parents were far removed from the glamor of the theatrical world. His father was a highly respected officer in the British Army during World War II, but at home, he was an abusive husband, and young Patrick had to helplessly witness repeated violence against his mother. Stewart wrote about his experiences with domestic violence in The Guardian in 2009. The stage, he confessed there, seemed to him "a far safer place" than reality; he saw acting as a way to escape his home life.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Patrick began acting at the age of 12. At 16, he left school early and, thanks to a scholarship, studied acting in Bristol, England. Along the way, he worked as a journalist. In 1965, he became an official member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, and remained with the theather company from 1966 to 1982. Such was his passion for the great English playwright and lyricist that he even shared his sonnets on his Twitter account during the 2020 coronavirus pandemic.

Stewart dazzled the theater world with his own stage adaptation of Charles Dickens' 1843 tale "A Christmas Carol." He played more than 30 roles himself. After its 1987 premiere in Stewart's hometown of Mirfield, the one-man show became a critics' favorite and a long-running hit on Broadway in Fresh York.

In the same year,  Stewart went from being a stage actor to an international TV star. Star Trek producer Robert Justman offered him the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, one of the main characters in a fresh edition of the popular TV series "Star Trek: The Next Generation.".

In a recent development, the successful Shakespearean hesitated. Until then, he had never worked in Hollywood. But his agent encouraged him to accept the role, Stewart recalled in a 2020 interview with the German newspaper Die Welt. "You can accept the offer as a start for now. It won't be a major deal, you can't revive a series as iconic as Star Trek anyway.".

In a recent development, but his agent was to be proven wrong: Stewart led the Starship Enterprise through its galactic adventures for seven seasons and four full-length feature films. The TV series had astronomical success on Earth in a very short time. At first, the producers were at odds as to whether Stewart's British accent could really fit the role of commander of a US starship in the 24th century, but it soon became impossible to imagine the series without the subtly diplomatic Captain Picard, who often quoted Shakespeare while at the helm. It seemed as if all the time he had spent as a Shakespearean actor had prepared him to command the Enterprise, Stewart once remarked with a wink. When the cult series ended in 1994, he had ruled out ever returning to the Enterprise's command center.

Recent findings suggest that in 2010, the actor was knighted by the Queen of England. Stewart considered it the greatest honor of his career to stand alongside acting greats such as Sir Laurence Olivier and Sir Alec Guinness.

Industry observers note that beyond the screen, Stewart has long used his voice for social and human rights causes. In recent years, he has drawn attention to concerns such as violence against women, age discrimination and the protection of children.

It has been revealed that in a June 2020 interview, "Playboy" asked the New York resident whether he was considering retiring from acting. "Never! That would mean giving up my life," replied Stewart, who was approaching his 80th birthday at the time. He was filming the second of three seasons of "Star Trek: Picard." The series ends with a final episode in which the retired Starfleet admiral makes his last appearance. In the series, Picard retires to his family vineyard in France but is drawn back into space to confront new threats to the Federation.

This series also showcases Stewart's affection for his pit bull, Ginger. In "Star Trek: Picard," Picard also has a pit bull, a loyal four-legged companion named Number One — a deliberate reference to Stewart's real-life love of the breed. For his efforts to combat prejudice against pit bulls and to support their adoption, Stewart was honored by the US animal welfare organization ASPCA, among others.

In 2024, he published his memoir "Making it So." In it, he recounts his passion for theater and his love of Shakespeare.

Now, at the age of 86, the British actor has finally departed for another galaxy. Farewell, Patrick Stewart!

Some grounds are beautiful. Some grounds are not so beautiful. Some grounds take you to the heart of the English game. And some leave you feeling like you're on the periphery.

But each of them holds the soul of their community and the hopes and dreams of the thousands of people who make the pilgrimage there every weekend.

Recent findings suggest that on April 1, 2025, I made the trip to Harrogate Town’s Exercise Stadium and first fulfilled the quest of a lifetime by completing the set of all 92 English Football League grounds for Daily Mail Sport. But then Everton moved away from Goodison Park and into a stunning new stadium on the banks of the River Mersey.

Industry observers note that I was one short again but on February 23, 2026, I got back up to 92 by going to Hill Dickinson Stadium to watch Everton versus Manchester United. Then, in November, with York City being promoted (alongside Rochdale, whose ground I had ticked off decades ago), I made the trip to the LNER Stadium to make the 92 whole again.

Recent findings suggest that I won’t give too much away just yet, but why are grounds like AFC Wimbledon and Exeter City in my top 20? What about Anfield, Old Trafford and Stamford Bridge? Where does Everton’s dazzling new home rank? Where is the best grub in the Premier League and where did Tyson Fury once threaten to have my jaw broken?

In a recent development, this is my love letter to English football. Read on to find out who comes out on top, where your team ranks and everything else in between – then let me know what you think of my guide to the 92 grounds of England.

Division: Championship Opened: 1993 Capacity: 19,369.

Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir.

It has been revealed that I’ve been banned from The Den for the last 20 months, in a professional capacity anyway. I could still go in a personal capacity but, on balance, I think I’d rather not.

The Daily Mail has been told that our reporters are not welcome at the club because we had the temerity to report on the horrendous challenge by Millwall goalkeeper Liam Roberts on Crystal Palace’s Jean-Philippe Mateta during the FA Cup tie at Selhurst Park in March last year, which left the French striker requiring 25 stitches in his left ear.

Sources indicate that let’s be honest about this: there are worse places to be banned from. Being banned from The Den is the football equivalent of being banned from your local abattoir. You don’t have to be a racist, misogynistic, homophobic bloke with anger concerns and a penchant for tragedy-chanting to feel at home at The Den. But it helps.

And, yes, I know Millwall are trying to rebrand themselves as a ‘family club’ now and the odd Tarquin and Tabitha stray across the county lines from Blackheath and Clapham to keep it real but that just makes The Den experience even worse.

The last time I went as a supporter was 16 years ago to watch Stockport County play there and the walk from South Bermondsey station to the away turnstiles was an eye-opener.

In a recent development, not that there were any problems: even at Millwall, football has moved on since the 70s. But this still felt deeply dystopian: for their own safety, away fans walk to the ground through a long wire mesh cage that seems to have no end. It felt like embarking on a tour of Jurassic Park: you know that if the fences fail, the dinosaurs are going to take a run at you.

Recent findings suggest that inside the ground, which is modern and neat and relatively characterless, the level of hatred for visiting supporters feels unusually visceral. It’s loud. I’ll give it that. It’s primeval. It’s unreconstructed, which can be a good thing, too, and it breeds a sense of togetherness.

If medievalism is your thing, you’re in for a treat. If not, give it a miss.

Division: League One Opened: 2007 Capacity: 30,303.

According to recent reports, I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons, for that matter.

Recent findings suggest that I know it’s a soft target but I really don’t care much for Stadium MK. Or for MK Dons themselves for that matter.

The club was born under a bad sign when it was jemmied out of Wimbledon and moved to Milton Keynes in 2003 and it has never been able to shake the stigma since. The stadium fits the club.

Sources indicate that it is a soulless, faceless, gloomy place. More than that, there is something rather forbidding about it. Its 30,000 capacity is too massive for the club it hosts and, apart from the joys of the local KFC and McDonald’s, there is little to recommend in its immediate surrounds. Its black seats lend it a sinister air, too.

Recent findings suggest that it’s the kind of stadium only its mother could love. And it doesn’t have a mother. Unless you want to do the 92, give it a miss.

Industry observers note that 90. Kassam Stadium, Oxford United.

Division: League One Opened: 2001 Capacity: 12,537.

The empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate.

I feel ashamed to say it, given that it is my local club, but the best experience I’ve had at the Kassam Stadium was getting my Covid jab there during the pandemic.

When they moved, around the turn of the century, abandoning the chaotic charm of the Manor Ground in Headington and swapping it for an isolated plateau outside the city, they only completed three sides, abandoning the fourth because of rising costs.

A particularly bitter wind blows in off the car park behind one of the goals and, from the main stand – in fact, from every stand – there is a magnificent and uninterrupted view of the Frankie and Benny's in the mini retail park that abuts the ground.

Industry observers note that the empty end kills a lot of the atmosphere, too, although the Oxford fans are to be commended for the noise they do generate given they have endured a generation of being stuck here. Firoz Kassam still owns the stadium but not the club. That kind of separation always spells trouble.

Oxford are hoping to move to a new stadium to the north of the city in a couple of years’ time. It can’t come soon enough.

89. London Stadium, West Ham United.

Division: Championship Opened: 2012 Capacity: 62,500.

It was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t even like calling it the London Stadium. It’s the Olympic Stadium, but it suited the David Sullivan-Karren Brady rebrand of the club to give it the capital’s name.

According to recent reports, it was a great athletics arena and home to a whole host of golden memories at London 2012 but it’s a dog’s dinner of a football ground. It’s also a monument to much that is wrong with the upper reaches of the English game: a surrender of identity and tradition as collateral damage in the owners’ pursuit of profit.

In a recent development, walking to it, sadly, feels a bit like walking through a wasteland and its odd configuration inside harms the atmosphere even though the fans are right up there with the best in the country. The old stadium at Upton Park was intimate and raucous and intimidating. The London Stadium is nothing like that.

The owners spent a lot of time congratulating themselves on the deal they did to move to the fresh ground: they’re the archetypes of football owners who know the price of everything and the value of nothing.

88. Hillsborough, Sheffield Wednesday.

Division: League One Opened: 1899 Capacity: 34,835.

It is hard to get past Hillsborough's association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and the betrayal of supporters.

I used to think of Hillsborough as one of the cathedrals of the English game but since the disaster that claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans in 1989, it is hard to get past its association with so much death and despair and heartbreak and betrayal of supporters.

I know, obviously, that this would punish Wednesday fans who do not deserve to be punished for something that had nothing to do with them but Hillsborough, and its Leppings Lane End in particular, has such a cursed legacy that part of me thinks it should have been demolished and that the club should have moved elsewhere.

Even in the last couple of years, fans of Newcastle United and Leeds United have reported serious safety concerns in the Leppings Lane End.

I recognise the flaws in my argument about demolishing the stadium, or part of it, and the emotions it provokes on all sides so perhaps it’s just enough to say I’ll never feel the same about the stadium as I once did.

Visiting it now feels like an intrusion.

Sources indicate that 87. Sixfields, Northampton Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1994 Capacity: 8,203.

Sixfields is a soulless ground anyway but its challenges have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

Sixfields is a blighted stadium.

It is a soulless ground anyway but its issues have been compounded by redevelopment delays and questions about missing money.

It has been revealed that it has the same kind of deracinated feel as so many of the newly introduced-build stadia pushed to the peripheries of towns. Its supporters deserve a lot better.

According to recent reports, 86. Broadfield Stadium, Crawley Town.

Division: League Two Opened: 1997 Capacity: 5,907.

But this stadium on a roundabout on the A12 in the middle of a retail park is still rather a bleak place to watch football.

Sources indicate that the empty corridors and the cavernous suites lent it a slight feel of the Overlook Hotel on the inside. On the outside, the four corners of the stadium are open, which makes for especially bitter nights in the winter.

The Bescot was the first of the generation of identikit newly introduced-build arenas I went to and there is not, frankly, much to recommend it apart from the loyalty of the fans.

The Croud Meadow is altogether more prosaic. Abutted by a McDonald’s and a TK Maxx on the outer fringes of the town, it feels like a disembodied place, separated from its community, functional but uninspired.

I was persona non grata for a while at the Select Car Leasing Stadium when I took exception to Reading taking out two Chelsea goalkeepers in one match back in 2006, when Steve Coppell and Wally Downes were in charge at the Madejski Stadium.

People called it the Mad Stad back then and I remember Neil Warnock telling me about being chased to his car outside the main entrance when he was manager of Sheffield United.

Anyway, I’ve made up with Stephen Hunt, who was one of the players involved in the tumult against Chelsea, and with Downes since then.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost character because the fans just merge into one.

Pride Park is the standard-bearer, sadly, for what is lacking in many of the new generation of English football stadia.

English football grounds should be about the North Bank and the Stretford End and the Kop and the Gallowgate End and the Shelf.

They’re supposed to be about defined areas that give a stadium character and personality and even rivalry among home fans about who sings loudest.

Too many of the modern bowls have lost that character because the fans just merge into one.

Industry observers note that this is not a criticism of Derby County fans in any way. They still make plenty of noise inside their stadium but the place is not a patch on the Baseball Ground, which witnessed so many momentous days and nights.

Recent findings suggest that I stood in the away end there with Manchester United fans in the early 80s but when I visited later in my life, the Vetch was locked up and derelict. If you peered through the gates, you could see small trees and shrubs growing on the pitch.

The Swansea.com Stadium lacks the same character, obviously, but it is a tight ground where the fans can still generate a rousing atmosphere if their team’s displays allow it.

Burton’s a fine club with a distinguished non-League history that can boast Neil Warnock and Nigel Clough as former managers and which has nailed down its place in the Football League.

One of the few times I was genuinely scared at a football stadium when I was a supporter was during a visit to Leicester City’s former stadium at Filbert Street.

In the crush to get out of the away end at the final whistle, I was lifted off my feet in the surge.

So I’m aware that there are limits to how much one should mourn the passing of that generation of stadia but I still find it hard to warm to arenas like the King Power.

It is comfortable and it is functional and the Leicester fans made plenty of noise in happier times but it’s a bland, featureless bowl that has little to distinguish it from many of the fresh generation of stadia.

Even then, it provided me with one of the great memories of the last decade when Andrea Bocelli stood next to Claudio Ranieri and sang Nessun Dorma the game after Leicester had pulled off the shock of the century by winning the Premier League in 2016.

EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

It is a high bar in these days when money counts a lot more than heritage and finances are fraught at the wrong end of the EFL, but the EV Charger Points Stadium may have the most chequered naming rights past of any stadium in the country.

We should just stick with Whaddon Road really but it was renamed the Abbey Business Stadium in 2009, then it became The World of Smile Stadium, then the LCI Rail Stadium in 2016–17, then the Jonny-Rocks Stadium in 2018–19, and the Completely-Suzuki Stadium in 2022 and now its current glorious and evocative name.

I hope they got a lot of money for those sponsorships because they make the club look stupid and cheap and rip chunks of its identity away from it.

In a recent development, again, I know it’s probably not financially viable to do away with them but I hate stadium naming rights. I’d ban them if I could. Football survived for a century without them, so why not now?

Division: League Two Opened: 2021 Capacity: 8,500.

David 'Bumble' Lloyd, England's former cricket coach and a broadcasting legend, is a season-ticket holder at York City. 'A grand stadium,' he noted of the ground the club moved to in January 2021 after 90 years at Bootham Crescent.

After York's promotion from the National League last season, it was the only ground of the 92 that I had not visited and I made my first trip there this month for the FA Cup first-round tie against Northampton Town.

The new stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

Recent findings suggest that I don't particularly warm to out-of-town stadiums built next to retail parks but York challenged that perception. Society is changing and town planning is changing. Retail parks are our upcoming high streets and if a club is to be at the heart of a community, there are worse places for it to be than beside a Hotel Chocolat, an M&S Foodhall, a multiplex cinema, a teaching hospital, a leisure centre and a bowling alley.

I'd paid my homage to Bootham Crescent earlier by visiting the housing estate where it once stood. A small part of the main stand and the players' tunnel has been preserved, which is, at least, a nod to the club's heritage but I wish there were more.

The fresh stadium is a little bit identikit for my liking and it was a shame that only two of the four stands were fully open but life is not easy in the lower leagues and York are making the best of it.

In a recent development, their crowds are still excellent and I got to witness the fastest goal I've ever seen, too. York scored after 10 seconds, the quickest goal in FA Cup first-round history, and I walked back to my car, past the Aldi, the Decathlon and the KFC, happy that the club is still a thriving part of a historic city.
